title: CourseAssist: Pedagogically Appropriate AI Tutor for Computer Science Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of using large language models as tutoring tools in computer science education while avoiding common risks such as overreliance, incorrect code generation, and answers that do not support learning. The authors argue that generic LLMs like GPT-4 may be useful but are not sufficiently aligned with course objectives or pedagogical needs, so they propose a more controlled, course-specific AI tutor.

The intervention studied is CourseAssist, a pedagogically oriented AI tutoring system built on GPT-4 with retrieval-augmented generation, user intent classification, and question decomposition. These components are intended to align responses with course materials, infer what kind of help the student needs, and provide hints or explanations rather than direct answers when appropriate. The system is compared against baseline GPT-4 on 50 question-answer pairs sampled from Piazza posts in a programming languages course at a large public university.

The study population is undergraduate computer science students in a real course setting, with evaluation involving an instructor scoring generated responses and interviews with 20 student users after deployment across 6 computer science courses at one large public R1 university. Results show that CourseAssist outperformed GPT-4 on usefulness, accuracy, and pedagogical appropriateness, and the authors conclude that course-specific guardrails and intent-aware retrieval can make LLM tutoring more educationally suitable for computer science instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a short conference poster with a small-scale human evaluation and interview evidence rather than a controlled experimental design. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but the methodology does not meet strong causal-credibility standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are positive but modest in scope and are based on a 50-item evaluation plus qualitative user feedback. No standardized learning outcome or effect size is reported, so the broader educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: CourseAssist, a GPT-4-based course-specific AI tutor for computer science education that uses retrieval-augmented generation, user intent classification, and question decomposition to provide pedagogically appropriate hints and answers aligned to course materials.

The paper positions CourseAssist as a tutor-like system and compares its behavior to instructional tutoring principles, but it is not a classical ITS; the ITS label is only a partial fit for its controlled tutoring functionality.

finding.finding_summary: On a human-evaluated set of 50 programming Q&A pairs from a computer science course, CourseAssist outperformed baseline GPT-4 on educational response quality. Mean scores were higher for usefulness (0.91 vs 0.83), accuracy (0.92 vs 0.71), and pedagogical appropriateness (1.00 vs 0.82), indicating better course-aligned tutoring support.
finding.measure: Instructor human ratings of usefulness, accuracy, and pedagogical appropriateness for generated responses

finding.finding_summary: Interviews with 20 student users suggested the system improved access to course-specific help and shortened the feedback loop on programming assignments. The paper reports deployment across 6 computer science courses reaching over 500 students, but does not provide a quantified effect size for time savings or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Student interview reports of access to tutoring help and feedback-loop speed
finding.study_size: n=20 interviewed users; deployment across 6 courses reaching >500 students
